theme: Oracles against Babylon, Assyria, Philistia, Moab [survey]
readingInstruction: Read Isaiah 13:1-17:14. This is a survey day. These chapters contain oracles against Babylon, Assyria, Philistia, Moab, Damascus, and others. Do not worry about every name. Read for the main point: God rules over all the nations.
settingTheScene: Isaiah’s message so far has been to Judah. Now he turns outward. The oracles against the nations make up chapters 13 to 23, and they teach that the God of Israel is not just a tribal deity. He is the judge of all the earth. Babylon and Assyria, the great powers of the day, are included. These oracles also served a purpose for Judah: they showed that trusting in alliances with the nations was foolish, since all of them are under God’s judgment.
observation: “The oracle concerning Babylon which Isaiah the son of Amoz saw” (13:1).
“Behold, the day of the LORD comes, cruel, with wrath and fierce anger, to make the land a desolation” (13:9).
“I will punish the world for its evil, and the wicked for their iniquity; I will put an end to the pomp of the arrogant” (13:11).
“How you are fallen from heaven, O Day Star, son of Dawn! … You said in your heart, I will ascend to heaven” (14:12-13).
“This is the purpose that is purposed concerning the whole earth, and this is the hand that is stretched out over all the nations” (14:26).
“For the LORD has had compassion on Jacob and will again choose Israel” (14:1).
“In that day man will look to his Maker, and his eyes will look on the Holy One of Israel” (17:7).
interpretation:
The first oracle is against Babylon, which at this time was not yet the dominant power. Isaiah looks ahead to its rise and fall. The day of the LORD is a day of judgment on pride, “to put an end to the pomp of the arrogant.” Babylon is described as “the glory of kingdoms,” yet it will be like Sodom and Gomorrah, a place for desert animals. In the Bible, Babylon becomes a symbol of human pride and organized rebellion against God, from the tower of Babel to the book of Revelation.

The taunt against the king of Babylon in chapter 14 is one of the most striking passages in Isaiah. The king is addressed as “Day Star, son of Dawn,” who tried to ascend to heaven and set his throne above the stars of God. He is brought down to Sheol. Christian tradition has often read this passage as describing Satan’s fall, and the pattern of pride that leads to a fall certainly applies. In its original setting, it is a mocking song about a tyrant whose arrogance ended in the grave. Either way, the lesson is the same. Whoever exalts himself will be humbled.

Notice that in the middle of the judgment, Isaiah describes God’s compassion on Jacob. God’s justice toward the nations is connected to his faithfulness to his people. And the purpose is “purposed concerning the whole earth.” History is not random. God has a plan, and none can annul it.

Even in the oracle against Moab, Isaiah weeps. “My heart cries out for Moab.” The prophet is not gleeful about judgment. And Damascus, Ephraim, and the others show the same: trust in human alliances will fail. In the day of judgment, people will “look to their Maker.” Some will turn to him.
connection: Jesus said, “I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven” (Luke 10:18). Revelation 18 describes the fall of Babylon the great, and Revelation 17 shows its pride. Daniel 4:30-37 shows Nebuchadnezzar humbled. James 4:6 says, “God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble.” Acts 17:26-27 says God made every nation and determined their times and boundaries. Ezekiel 33:11 shows that God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked.
application:
Look at the news and remember that God rules the nations. Pray for a nation that is in turmoil.

Examine yourself for the pride expressed in “I will ascend.” Where do you want to be on top?

Weep for someone you might be tempted to judge, as Isaiah did for Moab.
prayerPrompts: Praise God as ruler of all nations.
Ask him to humble pride in you.
Pray for a nation in turmoil.
